hook.line: Vale knows what she wants for herself, and she knows what she wants from Tomás. In Spanish those two wants sound different, and mixing them up changes who is doing what.
hook.es: Quiero quedarme, pero quiero que tú te quedes también.
hook.en: I want to stay, but I want you to stay too. (to a friend)

examples.en: I want to leave early today.
I want you to leave early today. (to a friend)
I don't want to sign anything.
I don't want you to sign anything. (to a friend)
Do you want to cook tonight? (to a friend)
Do you want me to cook tonight? (to a friend)

examples.es: Hernando quiere que le traigas un tinto.
examples.en: Hernando wants you to bring him a black coffee. (to a friend)

rule:
Before you choose, ask one question: who does the second thing?

The same person who wants it: plain dictionary form, no *que*.
*Quiero salir.* I want, I leave.
*¿Quieres cocinar?* You want, you cook.

Someone else: *que* plus the opposite vowel.
*Quiero que salgas.* I want, you leave.
*¿Quieres que cocine?* You want, I cook.

English hides the switch. I want to go and I want you to go look almost the same, with just a you in the middle. Spanish makes you rebuild the sentence: *que*, a new person, a new ending.

The mistake to avoid runs both ways. Never put *que* when it's the same person (*quiero que yo salga* sounds broken), and never leave the plain form when it's someone else (*quiero tú salir* doesn't exist).
smallPrint: Teachers call this the same subject or different subject rule: infinitive versus *que* plus subjunctive.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *dormir* or *que duermas* and type the whole sentence: *Quiero ___.* (I want to sleep.)
yourTurn.why: You want and you sleep: same person, so the plain form.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *ayudarme* or *que me ayudes* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Quiero ___.* (I want you to help me.)
yourTurn.why: You want, your friend helps: two people, so *que me ayudes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I need to talk to you. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: You need and you talk: one person, no *que*.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell a friend: I need you to talk to Hernando.
yourTurn.why: Your friend does the talking, so *que hables*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: Do you want me to cook tonight?
accept: ¿Quieres que cocine hoy en la noche?
yourTurn.why: Your friend wants, you cook: *que cocine*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change who does it. Now you want your friend to sign, not you: *No quiero firmar nada.*
yourTurn.why: A second person appears, so *que* and the opposite vowel: *firmes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change who does it. Now it's you who wants to learn: *Quiero que Simón aprenda otra frase.* (I want to learn another phrase.)
yourTurn.why: Back to one person, so drop *que* and use the plain form.

pitfalls.why: Almost. You want and you stay, so Spanish uses the plain form: *quedarme*.
When someone else stays, Spanish needs *que* and the new ending: *que te quedes*.
If you're the one leaving, there's no *que*: just *salir*.

personal: Write two true lines: one thing you want to do this week, and one thing you want someone else to do. Start both with *Quiero*.
